The flickering gas lamps followed a curve far into the distance. Outside a small house enclosed by walls stood a lone hansom cab, its driver sleeping inside. He hurried towards Portland Place, glancing behind him now and then as if afraid someone was following. At the corner of Rich Street, two men were reading a little notice pasted on a billboard. A peculiar curiosity drew him across the road. As he approached, he caught sight of the word ‘Murder’ in black print. He flinched, and his face flushed deeply. The notice offered a reward for information leading to the capture of a man of average height, aged between thirty and forty, wearing a bowler hat, a black coat, and checked trousers, and bearing a scar on his right cheek. He read it repeatedly, wondering whether the miserable man would be caught and how he had acquired the scar. Perhaps one day his own name would be posted on the walls of London. Perhaps there would be a price on his head too.

The thought filled him with a nauseating horror. He spun around and hurried away into the night.

He barely knew where he went. He vaguely remembered wandering through a maze of filthy houses, losing himself in an enormous web of gloomy streets. Dawn was already bright when he finally found himself in Piccadilly Circus. As he walked home towards Belgrave Square, he passed the great wagons heading for Covent Garden. Their drivers wore white smocks and had pleasant, sunburned faces and coarse, curly hair. They strode strongly along, cracking their whips and occasionally calling to one another. A plump boy sat on the back of a huge grey horse at the head of a jingling team, primroses tucked into his battered hat, his little hands gripping the mane as he laughed. Against the morning sky, the heaps of vegetables resembled masses of jade—green jade set against the pink petals of some extraordinary rose. Lord Arthur was strangely moved, though he could not say why. The delicate beauty of dawn seemed to him unbearably poignant. He thought of all the days that begin beautifully and end in storms. And these country people, with their rough, cheerful voices and easygoing manner—what an unusual London they witnessed! A city without the sins of night or the smoke of daytime, pale and ghostly, a deserted town of tombs. He wondered what they made of it, and whether they knew anything of its magnificence and disgrace, its fierce, flame-coloured pleasures and its terrible hunger, or all that it created and ruined between morning and evening.

But you will allow me two questions, will you not?”

“You may put them,” said Monks, appearing somewhat surprised; “whether I choose to answer is a separate question.”

“Which brings us to three,” remarked Mr. Bumble, attempting a little pleasantry.

“Is this what you supposed I should give you?” the matron asked.

“Yes,” Monks answered. “And the second question?”

“What do you intend to do with it? Could it be turned against me?”

“Never,” returned Monks; “nor against myself. Look here! But take one step nearer and your life won’t be worth a rush.”

As he spoke, he abruptly pushed the table aside, grasped an iron ring set in the floorboards, and flung back a broad trap-door. It opened almost beneath Mr. Bumble’s feet, sending that gentleman several paces backwards in extreme haste.

“Look below,” said Monks, letting the lantern down into the opening. “You needn’t fear me. Had I wished it, I could have dropped you through quietly enough while you sat over it.”

Reassured by this, the matron approached the edge; even Mr. Bumble, urged on by curiosity, dared to follow. Underneath, muddy water, increased by the heavy rain, raced past. Its splashing and swirling about the green, slippery piles swallowed every other sound. A water-mill had formerly stood below; the current frothed and fretted round the surviving rotten stakes and broken machinery, then seemed to leap forward with fresh force on escaping these barriers, which vainly sought to check its furious passage.

“Suppose you threw a man’s body down there—where would it be by morning?” Monks asked, swinging the lantern back and forth within the black shaft.

“Twelve miles along the river, and torn to bits into the bargain,” answered Bumble, shrinking from the notion.

Monks took the little parcel from his breast, where he had hastily concealed it. He fastened it to a leaden weight, once part of a pulley, which lay upon the floor, and let it fall into the current. It dropped straight and sure, split the water with a splash scarcely to be heard, and vanished.

The three exchanged glances, and appeared to breathe with greater ease.

“There!” Monks said, shutting the trap-door, which dropped heavily into place. “If ever the sea yields up its dead, as the books promise, it will hold on to its silver and gold, and to that rubbish with them. Our business is finished; we may dissolve this agreeable gathering.”

“Certainly,” said Mr. Bumble with remarkable readiness.

“You’ll hold your tongue, won’t you?” said Monks, looking at him menacingly.

All the young people were frantic to visit Lyme. Captain Wentworth spoke of returning there himself; the distance from Uppercross was only seventeen miles, and the weather, though it was November, was tolerably good. In brief, Louisa, the keenest of this eager party, had determined on the excursion. Besides enjoying the satisfaction of her own wishes, she now possessed the notion that perseverance in her chosen course was meritorious, and overcame every inclination of her parents to postpone the visit until summer. To Lyme, therefore, they would go: Charles, Mary, Anne, Henrietta, Louisa, and Captain Wentworth.

Their first unthinking proposal was to set out in the morning and come home that night; but Mr. Musgrove refused this, out of consideration for his horses. On sensible reflection, moreover, a day in mid-November would afford little opportunity to inspect an unfamiliar place once the seven hours demanded by the roads for the journey there and back were subtracted. They were accordingly to remain overnight and return only in time for dinner the following day. Everyone acknowledged this as a substantial improvement. Although they gathered at the Great House for a rather early breakfast and departed precisely on time, it was well after noon when their two carriages began the long descent into Lyme and entered the town’s even steeper street. The four ladies occupied Mr. Musgrove’s coach, while Charles drove Captain Wentworth in his curricle. Clearly there would be scarcely time to look about before the daylight and its warmth disappeared.

Once rooms had been obtained and dinner ordered at an inn, their next business was undoubtedly to walk straight to the sea. They had arrived too late in the season to enjoy whatever entertainments and diversions Lyme offered as a resort. The assembly rooms were closed, nearly every lodger had departed, and scarcely any households remained beyond those permanently resident. Since the buildings themselves offer little to admire, a visitor’s attention must seek the town’s striking position, its chief street seeming almost to rush into the waves; the path to the Cobb, following the curve of the agreeable little bay, which in season is lively with bathing machines and company; the Cobb itself, with its ancient marvels and recent improvements; and the lovely succession of cliffs extending eastward from the town. A most peculiar visitor it would be who found no attractions in Lyme’s immediate surroundings sufficient to inspire the wish for a closer acquaintance.
